\emph{This document is a structured, section-by-section summary of the key points argued in the companion manuscript, ``Three-component decomposition of treatment response in aggregated N-of-1 trials: pharmacological, expectation-driven, and natural-history components.'' It is provided as a supplementary reading aid and does not stand on its own; all notation, derivations, simulation detail, and citations are in the main manuscript.}

\bigskip\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.4pt}\bigskip

## A claim about how N-of-1 trials should be analyzed

\textbf{This paper argues that treatment response in N-of-1 trials comprises three causally distinct components that must be analyzed jointly rather than as a single indicator.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The three components are $BR$ (pharmacological), $PB$ (placebo-belief), and $TV$ (natural history).
\item Each component is causally distinct, clinically interpretable, and identifiable from a well-designed N-of-1 trial.
\item The standard single-indicator mixed-effects model conflates all three and renders biomarker validation unanswerable.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The contribution is the consolidation and extension of an established structural-decomposition tradition, not a novel decomposition.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The additive disease-progression, placebo, and drug-action decomposition is well established in pharmacometrics and longitudinal trial methodology.
\item The present framework extends that tradition with an explicit, separately identified placebo-belief channel and brings it to the aggregated N-of-1 setting.
\item The decomposition logic is not specific to N-of-1; it applies wherever a longitudinal treatment response is analyzed.
\end{itemize}

## Why this matters: three failure modes of the one-component analysis

\textbf{The one-component analysis has three documented failure modes that grow with unmodeled component heterogeneity.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The three failure modes are placebo-attribution bias, regression-to-the-mean, and biomarker-validation failure.
\item Each failure mode is documented in the chronic-condition trial literature, not merely hypothetical.
\item The failures are present regardless of sample size.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Placebo-attribution bias is sample-size-invariant and documented across antidepressant, anxiety, and IBS literatures.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Lumped treatment-effect estimates overstate pharmacological efficacy in proportion to $PB$ magnitude and variance.
\item Kirsch et al. and Locher et al. demonstrated that antidepressant apparent efficacy is largely explained by placebo response and natural fluctuation.
\item Placebo responsiveness has measurable biological correlates (e.g.\ COMT genotype), confirming it is a structured phenomenon, not noise.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Regression-to-the-mean contributes several points of apparent improvement in early trial weeks and is absorbed without trace by the one-component analysis.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Enrolment at peak severity guarantees a natural-history regression component irrespective of pharmacology.
\item Hrobjartsson et al.\ systematic reviews across 200+ trials showed much of conventional placebo response was indistinguishable from natural-history drift.
\item The one-component analysis has no formal mechanism to recover the pharmacological effect once regression is absorbed.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Biomarker validation is invalidated when a biomarker correlates with $PB$ or $TV$, rendering precision-medicine stratification wrong regardless of trial size.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item A biomarker correlated with placebo responsiveness or natural-history trajectory is indistinguishable from a true pharmacological predictor in a one-component analysis.
\item The PATH statement defers mechanistic attribution to domain knowledge; the BR-PB-TV decomposition supplies that substrate.
\item Where such coupling cannot be ruled out, rigorous pharmacological-biomarker validation requires the decomposition; where the biomarker is known orthogonal to $PB$ and $TV$, the one-component analysis already recovers the pharmacological slope.
\end{itemize}

## The current state of the N-of-1 literature

\textbf{The N-of-1 literature has matured substantially but motivates three observations that the present paper addresses.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The design has evolved from individual-patient consultation to a framework supporting population-level inference.
\item CONSORT reporting standards and quality audits document progressive improvement in analytic transparency.
\item Three specific gaps in the literature motivate the decomposition framework proposed here.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{No published N-of-1 trial employs a structural decomposition of treatment response despite three decades of methodological literature.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Audit data show the field has relied on paired t-tests, binary-indicator linear mixed-effects models (LME), and hierarchical Bayesian regressions.
\item Recent methodological advances (Liao 2023, Blackston 2019, Carrozzo 2025) retain the one-component response framing.
\item The decomposition gap persists even as carryover and identifiability problems are increasingly recognized.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Placebo-component separation is widely recognized but almost entirely unaddressed at the protocol level in N-of-1 methodology.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The Hendrickson hybrid blinded-discontinuation phase is among the few protocol mechanisms that supply $PB$-versus-$BR$ identifiability.
\item Placebo run-in, open-label-placebo, and mediator-analysis approaches have not been imported into N-of-1 designs.
\item The gap between awareness of the problem and protocol-level solutions motivates the present framework.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Kaptchuk's within-placebo decomposition is the closest structural analogue; no published paper applies the corresponding full-response decomposition to N-of-1 trials.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Kaptchuk et al.\ (2008) empirically decomposed the placebo response into observation, ritual, and relationship components.
\item Open-label placebo trials confirm that clinically meaningful PB-only response is possible even when patients know they receive placebo.
\item The BR-PB-TV framework is structurally analogous but operates at the level of the full treatment response.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The decomposition gap is real, the tools to fill it are mature, and the failure modes are large enough to make it a methodological priority.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The gap between available methodology and current practice is documented and not attributable to missing tools.
\item Failure modes in chronic-condition pharmacology are consequential, not academic.
\item The remainder of the paper develops, applies, and evaluates the decomposition framework.
\end{itemize}

## The neurobiological and epidemiological reality of the components

\textbf{Each component of the decomposition reflects a real causal mechanism documented in independent literatures.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item $BR$ corresponds to pharmacological action; $PB$ to neurobiologically real belief-driven mechanisms; $TV$ to natural-history drift.
\item The components are not statistical constructs but distinct causal pathways with separate literatures.
\item The section reviews the evidence for each component before establishing the formal model.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{$BR$ is the pharmacological target of regulation; $PB$ is neurobiologically real and phase-modulated, which is precisely the design contrast that makes the decomposition identifiable.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item $PB$ is mediated by endogenous opioid/dopamine release, HPA-axis regulation, and top-down attentional shifts.
\item Wager et al.\ neurologic pain signature provides a clean fMRI dissociation between pharmacological and expectancy contributions.
\item Phase-dependent belief variation (open-label vs.\ blinded) is the design contrast that supplies $PB$ identifiability.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{$TV$ is the untreated counterfactual trajectory; its heterogeneity is the central object of precision-medicine inference and must be modeled, not absorbed into noise.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item $TV$ sign depends on disease class: positive for acute recovery, near-zero for stable chronic, negative for progressive conditions.
\item Selection-driven enrollment at peak severity guarantees positive $TV$ in early trial weeks regardless of disease class.
\item The PATH statement identifies heterogeneity of treatment effects (HTE) modeling as mandatory for precision-medicine inference.
\end{itemize}

## What this paper contributes

\textbf{The paper makes four contributions spanning formalization, identifiability mapping, tractable methodology, and quantification of the inferential cost of the one-component analysis.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Sections 2--3 formalize the decomposition; section 4 maps it to design contrasts; section 5 develops tractable analysis methods.
\item Sections 6--7 provide worked examples and a Monte Carlo simulation study; section 8 applies the framework to biomarker validation.
\item A companion pedagogical document provides extended worked examples for first-time readers.
\end{itemize}

# Notation and the formal model

\textbf{This section fixes compact notation and states the formal model; a fuller worked-example treatment is in the companion pedagogical document.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Definitions are precise enough to support the identifiability and analysis-side arguments in later sections.
\item The presentation is kept compact; extended derivations are deferred to the companion document.
\item The companion pedagogical document provides numerical worked examples at each formal step.
\end{itemize}

where $Y_{it}$ is the observed symptom score, $\mathrm{BL}_i$
is participant $i$'s baseline score, the three components $BR$,
$PB$, $TV$ are non-negative reductions in symptom severity
attributable to the three causal mechanisms identified in
section 1, and $\varepsilon_{it}$ is observation-level noise.
The sign convention is that an increase in any component reduces
$Y$; all three components are zero at $t = 0$ by construction
(no exposure yet to drug, no belief activation, no elapsed
natural history) and grow over the duration of the trial.

\textbf{Each component is driven by its own time-on-state variable, making the components structurally distinct even when they overlap in calendar time.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item $BR_{it}$ accumulates with time-on-drug; $PB_{it}$ with time-on-belief scaled by expectancy $\eta(\text{phase})$; $TV_{it}$ with calendar time from trial entry.
\item The distinct time indices are the structural source of identifiability from phase-contrast data.
\item All components are zero at $t = 0$ by construction and grow over the trial duration.
\end{itemize}

rescaled so that $C(0) = 0$ and $C(t) \to m_C(1 - e^{-d_C})$ as
$t \to \infty$, for $C \in \{BR, PB, TV\}$. The three Gompertz
parameters $(m_C, d_C, r_C)$ are participant-specific random
effects drawn from population distributions, and the
participant-level heterogeneity in these distributions is the
principal source of between-participant response variability that the
framework is designed to characterize.

\textbf{The residual term has AR(1) structure and the three components are permitted to co-vary through cross-component covariances.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Within-participant residuals follow $\mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon_{it}, \varepsilon_{i,t+h}) = \sigma^2_\varepsilon \rho^{|h|}$.
\item Within-time and across-time cross-component covariances permit participant-level heterogeneity in one component to co-vary with the others.
\item This structure accommodates biologically plausible correlations, such as high-$BR$ patients also tending toward high-$PB$.
\end{itemize}

# The three components

\textbf{This section presents each component with its biological motivation, Gompertz parameterization, and identifiability conditions to establish the model as causally interpretable.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The three components are presented in turn: $BR$ (biological response), $PB$ (placebo-belief), $TV$ (natural history).
\item Each component is grounded in independent biological literature before its parametric form is stated.
\item The section's purpose is to demonstrate that the model sum reflects causal structure, not mathematical convenience.
\end{itemize}

## Biological response (BR)

\textbf{$BR$ is the pharmacological target of regulatory approval and biomarker stratification, independent of belief or natural history.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item $BR$ arises from chemical action on the body and is zero for inert pills regardless of patient expectation.
\item It is the estimand that approval decisions, dose selection, and biomarker-guided stratification require.
\item Separating $BR$ from $PB$ and $TV$ is the central precision-medicine problem the framework addresses.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) considerations produce a saturating $BR$ trajectory with a slow initial rise, a peak-growth phase, and a sharp drop to zero on discontinuation.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Plasma steady state is reached within a few half-lives; pharmacodynamic integration (e.g.\ receptor adaptation) adds additional lag.
\item For prazosin-PTSD, Raskind et al.\ (2013) calibrate the onset to several weeks of sustained exposure.
\item The saturating shape motivates the Gompertz over linear or simple exponential alternatives.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The three Gompertz parameters $(m_{BR}, r_{BR}, d_{BR})$ capture ceiling, onset rate, and climb shape respectively, calibrated to prazosin-PTSD reference values.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item $m_{BR}$ is the biological ceiling (maximum reduction at infinite exposure); $r_{BR}$ the onset rate; $d_{BR}$ the displacement shaping the early climb.
\item Prazosin-PTSD calibration yields $m_{BR} \approx 11$, $r_{BR} \approx 0.42$/week, $d_{BR} \approx 5$.
\item These are participant-specific random effects whose population distributions encode between-participant response heterogeneity.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The Gompertz is preferred over linear and simple-exponential alternatives because it captures the asymmetric slow-start saturation profile of chronic-condition pharmacodynamics.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Linear $BR = \beta t$ is biologically implausible past the first few weeks due to unbounded growth.
\item Exponential $BR = m(1 - e^{-rt})$ lacks the slow-start phase from receptor adaptation and gene-expression changes.
\item The Gompertz interpolates between both limits and its three-parameter form avoids overfitting; sensitivity analysis is reported separately in \texttt{07-gompertz-evaluation}.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{$BR$ is identified by the blinded-discontinuation contrast, where drug removal collapses $BR$ to zero while $PB$ remains intact.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Within-participant on-drug versus off-drug contrasts are the primary identification mechanism.
\item The blinded-discontinuation phase provides the cleanest contrast: $BR$ drops, $PB$ is preserved.
\item This contrast does not require the analyst to model $PB$ or $TV$ explicitly to recover $BR$.
\end{itemize}

## Placebo-belief response (PB)

\textbf{$PB$ is the strict placebo response: improvement that persists when the active drug is silently replaced, provided the patient's belief is unchanged.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item $PB$ is belief-dependent, not drug-dependent; it would survive a silent switch to placebo under sustained belief.
\item It is distinct from $BR$ in causal origin: $BR$ requires chemical action; $PB$ requires only belief.
\item The definition is strict and operational, not vague or colloquial.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{$PB$ reflects neurobiologically real mechanisms triggered by belief, not pharmacology; neuroimaging and genetic evidence confirm it is a structured biological phenomenon.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Belief-driven endogenous opioid/dopamine release, HPA-axis modulation, and top-down attentional shifts are all documented mechanisms.
\item Wager et al.\ neurologic pain signature dissociates pharmacological from expectancy contributions via fMRI.
\item COMT genotype predicts placebo responsiveness, confirming biological structure rather than measurement artifact.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{$PB$ is identifiable from $BR$ only when belief and treatment allocation differ, as in the blinded-discontinuation phase.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The blinded-discontinuation phase is the canonical contrast: patients cannot tell whether they remain on active drug.
\item Belief drops to a partial level ($\eta \approx 0.5$) because the patient's expectation is hedged, not absent.
\item Designs without a phase that decouples belief from treatment cannot separately identify $PB$ from $BR$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The $\eta = 0.5$ blinded-phase expectancy is a modeling assumption operationalizing response expectancy, not a measured quantity, and requires sensitivity analysis.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The construct is response expectancy in the sense of Kirsch (1985); to our knowledge the residual expectancy under blinded discontinuation has not been measured directly.
\item Open-label placebo trials confirm clinically meaningful $PB$-only responses even under explicit disclosure, bounding the residual response away from zero.
\item Sensitivity analyses varying $\eta$ are mandatory before clinical conclusions depend on this single parameter.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Kaptchuk et al.\ (2008) provide the structural precedent; the BR-PB-TV framework extends the same decomposition logic to the full treatment response.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Kaptchuk decomposed the placebo response itself into observation, ritual, and relationship components empirically.
\item The present framework applies analogous decomposition logic at the level of drug, placebo, and natural history.
\item Both frameworks reject the 'expectancy lump' model in favor of identifiable additive parts.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{$PB$ variance scales with $\eta$, not just its mean; ignoring this heteroscedastic structure miscalibrates standard errors and downstream biomarker tests.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Phase-dependent variance follows $\mathrm{SD}(PB \mid \text{phase}) = \eta(\text{phase}) \cdot \sigma_{PB}^{\text{baseline}}$.
\item Open-label phases have high between-participant $PB$ variance; blinded phases have low variance.
\item Ignoring heteroscedasticity deflates standard errors in open-label and inflates them in blinded phases, with consequences for CI coverage and biomarker test calibration.
\end{itemize}

### Additivity, subadditivity, and the BR-PB interaction

\textbf{Additivity is a modeling assumption, not biological fact; the section examines whether a $BR \times PB$ interaction term is warranted.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The formal model writes total response as a sum; this section asks whether the $BR$-$PB$ interaction is zero.
\item The question has inferential consequences for biomarker validation and for what the phase-augmented analysis captures.
\item The treatment is preparatory for the generalized interaction model introduced later in this section.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The additive model may be wrong: published literature documents subadditivity between pharmacological and placebo-belief effects in some clinical contexts.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Subadditivity means the combined $BR + PB$ effect is less than the sum of each component measured separately.
\item Evidence from Kaptchuk et al.\ and Benedetti et al.\ shows the phenomenon is context-dependent, not universal.
\item Formal test: $\partial Y / \partial(BR \cdot PB) > 0$ in a saturated mean-structure model.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Three candidate mechanisms for subadditivity are shared neural substrate, scale ceiling effects, and belief-dynamics adaptation.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Shared pain-modulation circuits produce saturating occupancy when both $BR$ and $PB$ activate them simultaneously.
\item Scale ceiling effects prevent registration of additional symptom reduction once $BR + PB$ saturates the measurement range.
\item Belief-dynamics adaptation: unexpectedly large $BR$ can recalibrate patient expectation downward, attenuating ongoing $PB$.
\end{itemize}

where $\gamma < 0$ encodes subadditivity, $\gamma = 0$ recovers
the additive form, and $\gamma > 0$ encodes superadditivity, is
the natural extension. The interaction coefficient $\gamma$ is
identifiable from the same trial-design contrasts that identify
the marginal components: open-label phases supply $BR \cdot PB$
products at high $\eta$, blinded phases supply $BR \cdot PB$
products at attenuated $\eta$, and the $\gamma$ coefficient is
estimated from the difference between the two regimes once the
marginal components are accounted for.

\textbf{Subadditivity biases biomarker predictive accuracy estimates and is partly absorbed by the phase-augmented analysis even without explicit $\gamma$ estimation.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Under subadditivity, the biomarker-by-$BR$ association is partly cancelled, inflating apparent predictive accuracy in the additive model.
\item Phase designs attenuating $PB$ (blinded, crossover) push the effective biomarker-treatment estimate closer to the true biomarker-by-$BR$ value.
\item The phase-augmented analysis in section 5 absorbs subadditivity as a side benefit.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{A forthcoming simulation study will quantify how bias in the biomarker-treatment interaction scales with $\gamma$; the pre-registration predicts linear scaling.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Bias in $\hat\beta_{bm:D}$ is expected to scale linearly with $\gamma$ at small $|\gamma|$.
\item Under subadditivity, bias sign is opposite to the true biomarker-by-$BR$ effect; under superadditivity it is aligned.
\item Empirical quantification is deferred to the production simulation program in section 7.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Non-zero $\hat{\gamma}$ does not establish true subadditive interaction; latent-class structure with class-correlated components produces the same marginal pattern.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item If class membership correlates with both $BR$ and $PB$ strength, the marginal covariance of $BR \cdot PB$ mimics a direct interaction term.
\item This confounding is invisible from the one-component analysis perspective but is identifiable in a class-aware analysis.
\item Apparent subadditivity can arise from latent population heterogeneity with no direct $BR$-$PB$ interaction in the class-conditional data-generating process (DGP).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Distinguishing true subadditivity from latent-class confounding requires either a class-aware analysis or the phase contrasts the BR-PB-TV framework provides.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The two mechanisms produce qualitatively similar marginal effects but are inferentially distinct.
\item $\hat{\gamma}$ should be reported alongside a class-aware sensitivity analysis, not as standalone evidence for mechanistic subadditivity.
\item The latent-class paper's \texttt{pb\_class\_correlation} simulation axis is the direct test; cross-paper synthesis is the cleanest disentanglement.
\end{itemize}

## Time-variant natural-history component (TV)

\textbf{$TV$ is the untreated counterfactual trajectory; it is participant-specific, structured, and can be positive, negative, or near-zero depending on disease class.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item $TV$ is the symptom change that would have occurred without treatment, integrated over the trial duration.
\item It varies in sign across disease classes and across patients within a class.
\item It is independent of treatment status and belief, distinguishing it structurally from $PB$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{$TV$ is a structured participant-specific signal, not noise; its distinguishing feature from $PB$ is independence from treatment status and belief.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Unlike $\varepsilon_{it}$, $TV$ is participant-level (slow trajectory) and requires explicit modeling, not absorption into noise.
\item Off-drug baselines and follow-up windows are the primary data sources for estimating $TV$.
\item $TV$ is modulated by neither treatment assignment nor patient belief, whereas $PB$ is modulated by both.
\end{itemize}

### When does natural history actually exist?

\textbf{The shape of $TV$ depends on disease class, trial timescale, and selection process; none of these can be assumed and all must be recovered empirically.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The assumption that subjects improve over time is true for some conditions and systematically wrong for others.
\item Disease class, trial timescale, and enrollment selection jointly determine the sign and magnitude of $TV$.
\item Recovering the empirical shape of $TV$ is one of the decomposition's primary objectives.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{$TV$ sign varies systematically by disease class: positive for acute recovery, near-zero for stable chronic, negative for progressive, and structured for cyclical conditions.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Acute conditions (post-operative pain, acute back pain) resolve intrinsically; substantial $TV$-improvement appears in the placebo arm.
\item Progressive conditions (Alzheimer's, ALS) require explicit negative-trajectory modeling; apparent treatment effect is slowing of progression.
\item Cyclical/triggered conditions (PTSD with trauma anniversaries, relapsing-remitting MS) require covariates beyond the Gompertz form.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Selection-induced $TV$ is real and rarely zero even for stable chronic conditions, because enrollment coincides with peak severity triggering help-seeking.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Regression to the mean alone contributes several points of apparent improvement in early trial weeks.
\item Hrobjartsson et al.\ systematic reviews across 200+ trials show much of conventional placebo response is indistinguishable from natural-history drift.
\item Kirsch (2008) and Locher (2015) demonstrate the clinical consequences in antidepressant and late-life depression trials.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Trial participation itself induces $TV$-improvement through Hawthorne, structured-visit, and diary-completion effects, independent of pharmacology or placebo.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Hawthorne, structured-visit, and diary-completion effects each contribute symptom improvements attributable to participation, not treatment.
\item These contributions are absorbed into $TV$ in the decomposition, not into $BR$ or $PB$.
\item Ignoring these participation-induced effects inflates the apparent pharmacological and placebo components.
\end{itemize}

### Can we assume no TV effect?

\textbf{Assuming $TV = 0$ is rarely safe in chronic psychiatric or pain trials; the conservative default is to estimate $TV$ from the data.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Zero-$TV$ assumption is valid only when all four conditions hold: stable disease, short trial, non-severity-peaked recruitment, no ancillary care.
\item For most chronic conditions at least one condition fails; the assumption should be tested, not asserted.
\item Statistical efficiency lost by estimating $TV$ is smaller than the bias introduced by assuming it zero.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The decomposition makes the zero-$TV$ assumption testable and shows that absorbing $TV$ into residuals produces autocorrelated, heteroscedastic residuals that bias $BR$ and $PB$ standard errors.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item $\hat{m}_{TV}$ with a variance estimate from the model provides an empirical test of the zero-$TV$ assumption.
\item Participant-level $TV$ is structured and correlated with the on/off-drug schedule; it is not independent noise.
\item Lumping $TV$ into $\varepsilon$ produces autocorrelated within-participant residuals and heteroscedastic cross-participant residuals.
\end{itemize}

### Why a Gompertz, not a linear time covariate?

\textbf{A linear \texttt{week} covariate is insufficient for $TV$ because it enforces linearity, ignores participant heterogeneity, and cannot distinguish $TV$ from $BR$ without the explicit decomposition.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item A \texttt{week} covariate constrains each additional week to contribute a fixed natural-history change, misrepresenting curved or saturating disease trajectories.
\item A single coefficient estimates a population-mean trajectory, ignoring participant-level heterogeneity in natural history.
\item Without the decomposition and design contrasts, \texttt{week} absorbs both $BR$ and $TV$, making them inseparable.
\end{itemize}

# Identifiability and trial-design contrasts

\textbf{Identifiability is supplied by trial design; each phase of the hybrid design contributes a different combination of components to the observed trajectory.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The decomposition is mathematically specified but requires trial-design contrasts to be statistically identified.
\item This section characterizes the hybrid open-label-plus-blinded-discontinuation design as the primary identifiability vehicle.
\item Each of the three phases supplies a distinct mixture of $BR$, $PB$, and $TV$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Three phase-by-allocation contrasts isolate $PB$, $BR$, and $TV$ respectively; the LME model combines them but the inference is driven by design.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Open-label versus blinded contrast yields approximately $0.5 \cdot PB$, isolating the belief component conditional on a known blinded-phase $\eta$.
\item Blinded on-drug versus blinded placebo yields $BR$ once drug carryover has elapsed (since $PB$ and $TV$ match across arms within the blinded phase).
\item Off-drug phases yield $TV$ plus residual off-drug $PB$, with no active $BR$ contribution beyond carryover.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Designs lacking specific phases lose identifiability of the corresponding component; the decomposition machinery is only as useful as the design allows.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item A pure open-label design cannot separate $BR$ from $PB$ because both are present at full strength throughout.
\item A pure blinded design cannot estimate $\eta = 1$ $PB$ because no phase achieves full-strength belief.
\item Trial designers should verify each component has at least one phase in which it is uniquely present before committing to the design.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Design-contrast identifiability is necessary but not sufficient: the three Gompertz trajectories are collinear, so joint estimation is credible only under specific design and sample-size conditions.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The components share an onset shape and overlap in calendar time, so their parameters can be near-collinear even when the identifying contrasts are present.
\item Joint recovery requires a phase in which each component varies while the others are held fixed, and an off-drug window long enough for $TV$ to separate from a decaying $BR$.
\item The recoverable region of the design-and-sample-size space is mapped by the pre-registered identifiability diagnostics, not asserted.
\end{itemize}

# Analysis-side methodology

\textbf{Four constraints make a component-matched analysis impractical at trial-relevant sample sizes; a phase-augmented LME captures the important part of the gap at minimal cost.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The question of whether to mirror the DGP in the analysis model is reasonable; the section addresses it directly.
\item The four constraints are identifiability, degrees of freedom, convergence fragility, and marginal estimand robustness.
\item A phase-by-treatment indicator is the recommended modest extension that captures BR-versus-PB sensitivity without the full parametric cost.
\end{itemize}

## Four reasons not to match the DGP

\textbf{The first constraint is identifiability: forcing a three-component model on a design with insufficient contrasts produces unidentified parameters, not component estimates.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item A pure open-label trial cannot distinguish $BR$ from $PB$; both rise from zero together on treatment initiation.
\item Fitting three components to a one-contrast design produces implausibly tight standard errors that misrepresent inferential precision.
\item The analyst must audit whether the design supplies the necessary contrasts before specifying a component-matched model.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The second constraint is degrees of freedom: a component-matched analysis adds approximately a dozen non-linear parameters, inflating moderation estimand variance at $N \in [30, 150]$.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Gompertz $BR$ (3), $PB$ (3 + expectancy multiplier), and $TV$ (3) each require participant-specific random effects on the maxima.
\item At trial-relevant $N$, the variance of $\hat\beta_{bm:D}$ is dominated by participant and timepoint counts.
\item Additional parametric structure typically inflates moderation estimand variance more than it reduces bias.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The third constraint is convergence fragility: component-matched nonlinear mixed models converge below 90\% at trial-relevant $N$, contaminating aggregated analyses.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Simultaneous Gompertz $BR$, $PB$, and $TV$ fitting requires \texttt{nlme::nlme}, Bayesian hierarchical, or structural-equation approximations.
\item Each is more sensitive to starting values, prone to local optima, and likely to fail on individual trial datasets than the LME analogue.
\item Non-converging cells at below-90\% convergence rates contaminate power and bias estimates in simulation studies.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The fourth constraint is estimand robustness: the \texttt{bm:Dbc} marginal interaction is the right estimand for the biomarker-validation question regardless of the BR-PB split.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Regulators want to know whether the biomarker predicts treatment response under trial conditions, not a mechanistically decomposed prediction.
\item The marginal \texttt{bm:Dbc} interaction captures this question whether the moderation is biological or expectation-mediated.
\item Component decomposition adds mechanistic precision but is not required for the core biomarker-validation decision.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The inferential target is stated as an estimand: the population biomarker-treatment interaction with explicit intercurrent-event handling, while the pharmacological-component target is more ambitious and inherits the heterogeneity-identifiability caveat.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The $bm{:}D_{bc}$ estimand is defined by its population, treatment contrast, endpoint, summary, and intercurrent-event strategy in the ICH E9(R1) sense.
\item Dropout is handled by a treatment-policy strategy and residual carryover by the modeled exponential decay.
\item Recovering a participant-level pharmacological interaction inherits Senn's caveat that true heterogeneity is separable from within-person variation only under repeated phase contrasts.
\end{itemize}

## A small extension that usually pays off: phase indicators

\textbf{The phase-augmented LME uses \texttt{Dbc:phase} and \texttt{bm:Dbc:phase} to test whether drug and biomarker-by-drug effects attenuate under blinding.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item \texttt{phase} absorbs systematic differences in $PB$ expectancy across trial phases.
\item \texttt{Dbc:phase} detects whether the drug effect shrinks under blinding, a signature of $PB$-mediation.
\item \texttt{bm:Dbc:phase} detects whether the biomarker-treatment interaction shrinks under blinding, a signature that it is partly biomarker-by-$PB$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The phase-augmented extension adds at most four parameters yet captures the practically relevant belief-attenuation diagnostic without requiring the Gompertz parametric form.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Three to four parameters is well within budget at any realistic trial sample size.
\item The extension does not separately estimate $BR$ and $PB$ components but identifies the change in apparent drug effect when belief is hedged.
\item For most analyses this is the practically relevant question and is answerable without committing to the Gompertz form.
\end{itemize}

## When to fit the full decomposition

\textbf{The full decomposition merits the effort only when $N$ is in the hundreds, the design is fully phase-balanced, and the scientific question requires the BR-PB mechanistic split.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Feasibility conditions: several-hundred $N$, dense timepoints in every phase, mechanistic BR-PB split required, and informative Bayesian priors available.
\item In that regime, \texttt{lcmm}, \texttt{nlme::nlme} with self-starting Gompertz forms, or \texttt{brms} can return participant-specific component estimates.
\item Outside that regime the phase-augmented LME is the better tool.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The DGP-analysis asymmetry is deliberate: simulation uses the rich DGP to characterize how a simpler analysis behaves; the analysis need not mirror the DGP to produce useful inference.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Simulation controls the DGP and can specify any structure; inference must pay the identifiability cost of every parameter.
\item The DGP is a characterization tool; the analysis is a finite-data inference tool; they have different optimality criteria.
\item DGP-matching is not required and is often counterproductive at trial-relevant sample sizes.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The exponential-decay carryover indicator is a deliberately parsimonious special case of richer carryover models, and the simulation should benchmark it against a distributed-lag alternative.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The continuous indicator $D_{bc}$ decays as $\exp(-\lambda t_{sd})$, a one-parameter form tied to a pharmacokinetic half-life.
\item Distributed-lag models, the average-period-treatment-effect estimand, and G-estimation relax the single-rate assumption at additional parametric cost.
\item The exponential restriction is an assumption, not a finding, and the pre-registered simulation should include a distributed-lag arm to quantify its cost.
\end{itemize}

## What the one-component analysis estimates

\textbf{The one-component treatment-effect estimate has a probability limit equal to the pharmacological component plus belief and natural-history contributions, so its bias does not vanish as $N$ grows.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Writing the reduction as $BR + PB + TV - \varepsilon$ and fitting one drug indicator gives $\operatorname{plim}\hat\beta_D = m_{BR} + b_{PB} + b_{TV}$.
\item $b_{PB}$ and $b_{TV}$ are the belief and natural-history terms that load onto the drug indicator under the chosen contrast; both are generally non-negative for an improving outcome.
\item Because the displacement is in the probability limit, a larger one-component trial converges on the same biased value: the failure is identification, not precision.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The biomarker slope from a one-component analysis decomposes additively into component-specific slopes, so a biomarker correlated with $PB$ or $TV$ registers as a predictor even with no pharmacological association.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item By linearity of covariance, $\beta_{bm}^{\text{lumped}} = \beta_{bm}^{BR} + w_{PB}\beta_{bm}^{PB} + w_{TV}\beta_{bm}^{TV}$.
\item A non-zero $\beta_{bm}^{PB}$ or $\beta_{bm}^{TV}$ produces a non-zero one-component slope even when the pharmacological slope $\beta_{bm}^{BR}$ is exactly zero.
\item The result is an algebraic identity under the additive decomposition, not a sample-size-dependent tendency.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The bias displaces the estimand rather than inflating variance, so a significance test of the one-component coefficient cannot detect it; the decomposition is what locates it.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The one-component coefficient is displaced from $m_{BR}$ by $b_{PB} + b_{TV}$ but remains a well-estimated quantity with a valid Wald test of its own nullity.
\item Detecting the bias requires comparing $\hat\beta_D$ to $m_{BR}$, a comparison only the decomposition or an isolating phase contrast supplies.
\item This is why a rejection-rate summary is the wrong instrument, and accounts for the flat rejection rates across the placebo-strength axis in the section 7.1 pilot.
\end{itemize}

## A numerical illustration

\textbf{The worked example uses two participants with identical one-component responses but opposite BR-PB profiles to show that the one-component analysis cannot distinguish them.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Participant A has high $PB$ ($m_{PB} = 6$) and moderate $BR$ ($m_{BR} = 4$); Participant B has low $PB$ ($m_{PB} = 1$) and high $BR$ ($m_{BR} = 8$).
\item Both participants reach approximately 10--11 points of total improvement by week 8, making them indistinguishable to a one-component analysis.
\item The blinded-discontinuation phase creates the diagnostic contrast that exposes the underlying difference.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Open-label totals are clinically indistinguishable; the one-component analysis estimates a population drug effect of approximately 10 points with no differentiation between A and B.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Both participants show approximately 10--11 points of improvement and present as clinical successes.
\item A t-test or simple LME on open-label change cannot detect the heterogeneity in $BR$ versus $PB$ composition.
\item The population drug-effect estimate conflates both pharmacological and placebo contributions.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The blinded-discontinuation phase reveals the BR-PB heterogeneity: Participant A retains 4 points while B collapses to 1.5, exposing the diagnostic contrast.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Participant A's high $PB$ at $\eta = 0.5$ (3 points) sustains improvement even without active drug.
\item Participant B's low $PB$ (0.5 points) and absent $BR$ produce near-complete return to baseline.
\item The 4.0 versus 1.5 contrast is exactly what the decomposition uses to separate $BR$ from $PB$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The one-component model estimates drug at 7.75 points with no principled decomposition, obscuring that A's true $BR$ is 4 and B's is 8.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The 7.75 point estimate is a conflated average of true $BR$ values (4.0 and 8.0) plus the placebo wash-out.
\item The model cannot determine whether A and B differ, nor estimate the pharmacological drug effect separately.
\item Placebo and natural-history effects are not identifiable from this contrast alone.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The full decomposition recovers all six component estimates by exploiting phase differential expectancy and the blinded-placebo contrast.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The LME returns $\hat{m}_{BR}^A = 4.0$, $\hat{m}_{BR}^B = 8.0$, $\hat{m}_{PB}^A = 6.0$, $\hat{m}_{PB}^B = 1.0$ at the population point estimate.
\item Participant-level estimates have meaningful uncertainty at trial-relevant $N$; the simulation study characterizes this.
\item The phase differential ($\eta = 1$ vs.\ $\eta = 0.5$) is the identification mechanism for the $PB$ parameter.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The one-component model produces one biased average; the three-component model produces six clinically actionable quantities, making biomarker validation possible.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The one-component estimate of 7.75 points is a biased average of $BR_A = 4$ and $BR_B = 8$ confounded with placebo wash-out.
\item The decomposition supplies individual $BR$, $PB$, and $TV$ estimates enabling per-participant clinical decisions.
\item Predictive-biomarker validation requires the decomposition because biomarker-by-$BR$ is the target estimand.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{A population-level example shows that cohort differences in open-label totals driven entirely by $PB$ produce apparent non-replicability that the decomposition resolves.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Cohort 1 (naive, $m_{PB} = 7$) reports 13-point improvements; Cohort 2 (skeptical, $m_{PB} = 2$) reports 8 points; true $m_{BR} = 5$ in both.
\item A one-component analysis would falsely conclude the drug works less well in Cohort 2 and trigger searches for confounders.
\item The decomposition returns $\hat{m}_{BR} = 5$ in both cohorts, attributing the difference correctly to $PB$ heterogeneity.
\end{itemize}

# Simulation study

\textbf{The simulation study follows ADEMP and quantifies bias and identifiability properties of three analysis strategies across a prazosin-PTSD-calibrated parameter grid.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The Morris (2019) ADEMP framework structures the study: Aims, DGP, Estimands, Methods, Performance measures.
\item The pre-registration is at \texttt{analysis/scripts/component-decomposition/00-ademp-pre-registration.md}.
\item Three analysis strategies (one-component, phase-augmented, full decomposition) are compared across the parameter grid.
\end{itemize}

## Pilot validation of analysis machinery (100 replicates, 6 cells)

\textbf{The pilot is a structural check of the analysis pipeline, not a substantive empirical result.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The realized Study A run (section 7.3) is the empirical core of the manuscript; this pilot precedes it.
\item The pilot confirms only that data generation, model fitting, and summary output run without error.
\item No bias or power claims are derived from the 100-replicate pilot.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The pilot executed a 6-cell, 100-replicate run with perfect convergence, confirming the pipeline is operational.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The grid crossed three $pb\_strength$ levels against two analysis strategies.
\item Convergence was 1.0 across all six cells under 8-core \texttt{mclapply}.
\item Output is checkpointed at \texttt{analysis/data/quick-sim/}; no inferential claims are drawn.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Two pilot findings revise the production specification: rank-deficiency forces a formula change, and bias must be read from coefficient means, not rejection rates.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item At $N = 35$, rank-deficiency dropped the $D_{bc}{:}\text{phase}$ term, eliminating the key biomarker-treatment-by-phase contrast.
\item The predicted bias manifests in the mean of $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$, not in the Wald-test rejection rate.
\item The production program addresses both by using larger $N$, a fuller design, and coefficient-mean reporting.
\end{itemize}

## Production-simulation specification

\textbf{The production program follows the ADEMP framework with four deliverables; the realized Study A run in section 7.3 is the first of these.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The deliverables are interaction-estimate bias, full-decomposition identifiability, Type I error and power, and participant-level signal recovery.
\item Sample sizes $N \in \{35,70,200,300\}$ cross a $pb\_strength$ grid; Type I cells target MCSE $0.003$ at 5{,}000 replicates.
\item Driver scripts, checkpointed outputs, and the ADEMP pre-registration reside under \texttt{analysis/scripts/component-decomposition/}.
\end{itemize}

## Study A results: bias and power at 1,000 replicates per alternative cell

\textbf{At 1,000 replicates per alternative cell the one-component estimate of $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ is essentially unbiased across the entire $(m_{PB}, m_{TV})$ grid, contradicting the framework's prediction of a placebo-strength-driven bias.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The true biomarker-by-$BR$ effect is $-2.25$; mean absolute bias is $0.016$ at $N=35$, $0.016$ at $N=70$, $0.006$ at $N=200$, and $0.006$ at $N=300$, in every case within one MCSE of zero.
\item Bias shows no monotone trend across $m_{PB} \in \{0,1,3,6,10\}$ or $m_{TV} \in \{-1,0,1,2\}$; it behaves as sampling noise around zero.
\item This is the predicted consequence of the identity in section 6.1: the DGP couples the biomarker to $BR$ only, so $\beta_{bm}^{PB} = \beta_{bm}^{TV} = 0$ and the one-component slope is unbiased by construction.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The phase-augmented analysis provides no bias reduction and incurs a substantial power penalty, so it is dominated under this uncontaminated DGP.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Mean power at $N=35$ is $0.35$ (phase-augmented) versus $0.59$ (one-component); at $N=70$, $0.62$ versus $0.90$; both reach approximately $1.0$ by $N=200$.
\item Phase-augmented mean absolute bias is no smaller than one-component at any $N$ ($0.028$ versus $0.016$ at $N=35$).
\item Convergence is approximately 100\% for both analyses at every $N$ (minimum $0.998$), so the rank-deficiency that degraded the $N=35$ pilot does not recur here.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Study A confirms the identity but cannot exhibit the biomarker-validation failure; a contaminated-biomarker pilot reported in the next subsection provides the decisive evidence.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item As pre-registered, Study A varies component magnitude with the biomarker fixed to $BR$, so it probes an axis the identity predicts to be null.
\item The decisive axis is $c_{bm,PB}$, the biomarker-$PB$ correlation; this is varied in the contaminated-biomarker pilot below.
\item On current evidence the phase-augmented analysis is not recommended for the uncontaminated-biomarker regime; the pilot below evaluates it under contamination.
\end{itemize}

## Contaminated-biomarker pilot (100 replicates per cell)

\textbf{A pilot varying the biomarker-$PB$ correlation $c_{bm,PB}
\in \{0, 0.15, 0.30, 0.45\}$ confirms that bias in the
one-component estimator scales with coupling strength, not
component magnitude, and that the phase-augmented analysis
provides no protection.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item At $N=300$, mean $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ shifts from
  $-2.25$ (true) to $-1.74$ at $c_{bm,PB}=0.45$ (bias $+0.51$,
  30 MCSEs from zero), confirming the identity's
  prediction.
\item The bias is driven by $c_{bm,PB} \times \sigma_{PB}$, not
  by the population-mean $m_{PB}$: cells with $m_{PB}=0$ and
  $m_{PB}=6$ show identical bias at every $c_{bm,PB}$ level,
  because the individual-level $PB$ variance ($\sigma_{PB}=2$)
  provides the contamination channel even when the mean is zero.
\item The phase-augmented analysis shows the same bias as the
  one-component analysis at every contamination level, offering
  no protection against biomarker-$PB$ coupling.
\item This pilot uses 100 replicates per cell; a production run
  at 1,000 replicates per cell is required to confirm the pattern
  and assess Type I error under contamination.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The contaminated-biomarker pilot reframes the paper's
practical guidance: the risk of biomarker-validation failure
arises from biomarker-$PB$ correlation in the study population,
not from the presence of strong placebo response per se.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item A trial in a population where the biomarker is uncorrelated
  with placebo responsiveness can use the one-component estimator
  without bias, regardless of how large the placebo response is.
\item A trial where the biomarker covaries with optimizm,
  suggestibility, or treatment-seeking history is at material
  risk of contamination; bias of $+0.51$ ($23\%$ of the true
  effect) at $c_{bm,PB}=0.45$ illustrates the practical scale.
\item Neither the one-component nor the phase-augmented analysis
  removes this bias; full component decomposition is required.
\end{itemize}

## Study B: recovery under a belief-decoupling design

\textbf{Study B shows the contamination is removable, but only under a design that decouples drug exposure from belief: on a balanced-placebo design a belief-covariate decomposition recovers the unbiased pharmacological slope across the contamination range, while the one-component estimator does not.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item On the standard hybrid design the drug state $D_{bc}$ and the expectancy $\eta$ are collinear, so no decomposition can separate the channels; we confirmed that several tractable decompositions fail there, no better than the one-component analysis.
\item A balanced-placebo design adds a covert on-drug phase (drug given, belief withheld, $\eta=0$) and an open-placebo phase (drug withheld, belief sustained, $\eta=1$), which decouples $D_{bc}$ from $\eta$.
\item The decomposition $Y \sim bm + t + D_{bc} + \eta + bm{:}D_{bc} + bm{:}\eta$ then isolates $\beta_{bm}^{BR}$ on the $bm{:}D_{bc}$ term while $bm{:}\eta$ absorbs the placebo channel.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{At 1{,}000 replicates per cell on the balanced-placebo design, the decomposition is essentially unbiased across the contamination range while the one-component estimator degrades monotonically.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item At $N=300$, the decomposition's bias of $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ stays within one MCSE of zero across $c_{bm,PB} \in \{0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$ ($-0.022$, $+0.008$, $+0.021$, $-0.026$; MCSE $\approx 0.02$), while the one-component bias rises monotonically to $+0.16$, $+0.34$, $+0.48$.
\item Nominal-95\% coverage is near-nominal for the decomposition ($0.94$--$0.96$) and falls to $0.86$ for the one-component analysis at the highest contamination; convergence is 100 percent for both.
\item The contamination grid is capped at $c_{bm,PB}=0.30$ because beyond approximately $0.45$ the implied covariance is non-positive-definite (minimum eigenvalue $-0.35$ at $0.45$) and the contaminated DGP is no longer faithfully representable.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Recovery is therefore conditional on the design, not on the analysis alone: the decomposition is necessary but the belief-decoupling design is what makes the pharmacological slope identifiable.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The practical implication is that a biomarker-validation trial exposed to possible biomarker-$PB$ coupling should adopt a balanced-placebo or open-hidden design, not the standard hybrid design, if the pharmacological interaction is to be recovered.
\item This sharpens the framework's central claim: decomposition is the mechanism, but a design that varies belief independently of drug exposure is the enabling condition.
\item Open questions remaining: recovery beyond the positive-definite range, the participant-level component recovery of the original Study B identifiability aims, and replication of the pattern under the mean-moderation architecture (mean-moderation) coupling.
\end{itemize}

# Application to predictive-biomarker validation

\textbf{The precision-medicine question -- whether a biomarker predicts pharmacological response -- is answered by the one-component total only when the biomarker is uncorrelated with $PB$ and $TV$; otherwise it requires decomposing the response.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The question is whether the biomarker predicts the $BR$ component, not the one-component total.
\item The PATH statement formalizes this as the target estimand for predictive biomarker validation.
\item The BR-PB-TV decomposition is the mechanism that separates the pharmacological signal when biomarker-component coupling cannot be ruled out.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{A one-component-total biomarker regression conflates pharmacological and placebo-belief prediction, producing a stratification biomarker that mis-identifies responders.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item $\hat\beta_{bm}$ from the one-component regression contains both pharmacological and placebo-belief prediction in unknown proportions.
\item If $PB$ covaries with the biomarker distribution, flagged 'high responders' include high-$PB$ responders who will not benefit pharmacologically.
\item Prospective application of such a biomarker would systematically mis-stratify patients for prescription decisions.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{A valid pharmacological predictor requires a non-zero $\hat\beta_{bm}^{BR}$; significant $\hat\beta_{bm}^{PB}$ or $\hat\beta_{bm}^{TV}$ indicate a psychological or prognostic biomarker, not a pharmacological one.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The sole criterion for pharmacological prediction is a meaningfully non-zero $BR$-component regression coefficient.
\item A biomarker correlating only with $PB$ selects placebo responders, not drug responders.
\item A biomarker correlating only with $TV$ is prognostic but not predictive in the pharmacological sense.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{When biomarker-component coupling cannot be ruled out, the decomposition is the mechanism by which the precision-medicine question is posed; when it can, the one-component analysis already answers it.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Where the biomarker may correlate with $PB$ or $TV$, separating $BR$ from them is what prevents validation from conflating pharmacological and non-pharmacological prediction.
\item The phase-augmented \texttt{bm:Dbc:phase} interaction is a small-$N$ proxy, but Study A shows it buys nothing under an uncontaminated biomarker, so it is warranted only when contamination is plausible.
\item The full decomposition recovers component-specific regressions explicitly when sample size permits.
\end{itemize}

# Discussion

\textbf{The three-component framework reframes treatment response as a structured sum of causally distinct contributions, and the present work maps when acting on that decomposition actually changes inference.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The framework specifies which trial-design contrasts identify which components.
\item Acting on the decomposition is valuable conditionally: for attribution estimands, and for biomarkers that may correlate with $PB$ or $TV$, but not for a biomarker-treatment interaction with a biomarker orthogonal to them.
\item The target estimand for biomarker validation is the biomarker-by-$BR$ association; whether a one-component analysis already recovers it depends on the biomarker's coupling to $PB$ and $TV$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Four open questions bound the framework's current scope: the simulation results are pending, the $\eta$ multipliers require sensitivity analysis, non-monotone natural history is not yet handled, and participant-level recovery inherits the identifiability caveats of individual treatment effects.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Quantitative bias-versus-power trade-offs are conjectures until the section 7 simulation is run.
\item The $\eta(\text{phase})$ expectancy-modulation parameters are modeling assumptions requiring explicit sensitivity analysis.
\item Cyclical or biphasic $TV$ trajectories exceed the Gompertz form and require flexible or covariate-augmented specifications.
\item Participant-level component recovery rests on separating participant-by-component signal from participant-by-period and participant-by-phase variation, the identifiability caveat Senn raises for individual treatment effects.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Two companion documents extend the manuscript: a pedagogical narrative and a Gompertz-family sensitivity evaluation.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The pedagogy document at \texttt{docs/24-component-decomposition-pedagogy.md} provides worked examples for first-time readers.
\item The Gompertz evaluation at \texttt{analysis/report/07-gompertz-evaluation/} quantifies trajectory-specification sensitivity.
\item Together they address the intuitive and parametric dimensions of the framework that the present manuscript treats briefly.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The components exist in any longitudinal treatment response, but participant-level identifiability requires a within-subject belief-by-exposure contrast that not every placebo-controlled design supplies.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The three-component structure is a property of the DGP of any repeated-measures treatment study; its identifiability is design-specific.
\item Parallel-group placebo control identifies the population-mean $PB$ but not a participant-level $PB$, and supplies no within-subject belief contrast; only designs with such a contrast (blinded or open-hidden discontinuation, randomized withdrawal, crossover, hybrid N-of-1) identify the participant-level decomposition the biomarker question needs.
\item The broad claim is therefore scoped to designs supplying a within-subject belief-by-exposure contrast, not to placebo-controlled longitudinal trials in general.
\end{itemize}

# Conclusions

\textbf{Treatment response in aggregated N-of-1 trials is the sum of three causally distinct components, and the bias from conflating them is governed by the estimand and the biomarker's coupling to the components, not by their raw magnitude.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The three components are $BR$ (pharmacological), $PB$ (placebo-belief), and $TV$ (natural history).
\item Each has its own biological mechanism, identifiability conditions, and clinical interpretation.
\item The one-component pre-post treatment effect is biased by the $PB$ and $TV$ contributions; the biomarker-treatment slope is biased only by the biomarker's covariance with $PB$ and $TV$, as Study A confirms.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{What matters is the design contrast, not the parametric model: the trial must supply the drug-on/off and belief contrasts, but adding parametric component terms is not free and is not always worth it.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Unique component identification requires phase contrasts built into the trial design; the one-component analysis already exploits the drug-on/off contrast.
\item Under an uncontaminated biomarker, the phase-augmented analysis adds no bias reduction and loses power, so it is not recommended as a default.
\item The phase-augmented and full component-matched analyses are warranted for attribution estimands and for biomarkers that may correlate with $PB$ or $TV$, where the extra structure does work.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{For predictive-biomarker validation the decomposition matters precisely when the candidate biomarker may correlate with $PB$ or $TV$; the contaminated-biomarker study demonstrates this failure and Study B shows it is recoverable under a belief-decoupling design.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item A biomarker that predicts the one-component total is a pharmacological predictor only if it is uncorrelated with $PB$ and $TV$; otherwise the one-component slope is contaminated.
\item Regulatory and prescribing decisions therefore require separating $BR$ from $PB$ and $TV$ whenever biomarker-component coupling cannot be ruled out.
\item Study A established the uncontaminated baseline, the contaminated-biomarker study (section 7.4) demonstrated the failure, and Study B (section 7.5) showed the bias is recoverable on a balanced-placebo design but not on the standard hybrid design.
\end{itemize}

# Reproducibility

\textbf{The manuscript is rendered inside a Docker container with locked package versions; the full software environment is pinned by \texttt{Dockerfile} and \texttt{renv.lock}.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item R 4.4.x in the zzcollab Docker container provides the execution environment.
\item Simulation packages are \texttt{nlme}, \texttt{parallel}, \texttt{data.table}, \texttt{furrr}, and \texttt{purrr}.
\item The manuscript build uses \texttt{rmarkdown} and \texttt{bookdown}.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Reproducibility is ensured by a master seed of 20260507 with per-replicate seeds derived by index addition.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item \texttt{set.seed(20260507)} is called at the top of each replicate loop.
\item \texttt{parallel::mc.set.seed} propagates seeds inside \texttt{mclapply}.
\item Per-replicate seeds are \texttt{master\_seed + rep\_idx}.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{All simulation outputs, driver scripts, pre-registration, and manuscript source files are versioned at documented paths within the repository.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Per-replicate outputs and Morris summaries are at \texttt{analysis/data/quick-sim/}.
\item Driver scripts and the ADEMP pre-registration are at \texttt{analysis/scripts/component-decomposition/}.
\item Manuscript source, bibliography, and CSL file are at \texttt{analysis/report/06-component-decomposition/}.
\end{itemize}
